notes:
d-Block: General Trends

  • General electronic configuration $(n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{0-2}$. Exceptions: Cr = $3d^54s^1$, Cu = $3d^{10}4s^1$ (extra stability of half-filled/fully-filled d subshell).
  • Atomic/ionic radii decrease across a period (increasing nuclear charge) but decrease is small in the middle due to d-orbital (shielding) effects; radii of 4d and 5d elements in a group are very close due to lanthanoid contraction.
  • Ionization enthalpy generally increases across a period (irregular due to stable $d^0,d^5,d^{10}$ configurations); first IE of 5d > 4d $\approx$ 3d generally.
  • Variable oxidation states are characteristic (both $(n-1)d$ and $ns$ electrons involved); most stable/common state often +2 or +3; Mn shows the widest range (+2 to +7); highest oxidation state = +8 seen in Ru and Os.
  • Coloured ions arise from d-d transitions (partially filled d orbitals); $Sc^{3+}(d^0)$ and $Zn^{2+}(d^{10})$ are colourless/white.
  • Paramagnetism increases with number of unpaired electrons; magnetic moment $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM.
  • Catalytic activity due to variable oxidation states and ability to form intermediates/provide large surface area (e.g. Fe in Haber process, V$_2$O$_5$ in Contact process, Ni in hydrogenation).
  • Form alloys (similar atomic size) and interstitial compounds (small atoms like H, C, N occupy interstitial voids — hard, high melting, chemically inert, e.g. steel, TiC).

Important Compounds

CompoundPreparationKey property
KMnO$_4$Fusion of MnO$_2$ with KOH + oxidant, then electrolytic oxidation of manganateStrong oxidiser; in acidic medium Mn$^{7+}\to$Mn$^{2+}$ (5e$^-$); in neutral/faintly alkaline Mn$^{7+}\to$Mn$^{4+}$ (MnO$_2$, 3e$^-$)
K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$From chromite ore FeCr$_2$O$_4$ via sodium chromate, acidifiedOrange, strong oxidiser in acidic medium (Cr$^{6+}\to$Cr$^{3+}$, 6e$^-$ per Cr$_2$O$_7^{2-}$); chromate $\leftrightharpoons$ dichromate interconversion is pH dependent (yellow in base, orange in acid)

Lanthanoids & Actinoids

  • Lanthanoids (4f, Ce-Lu): common oxidation state +3; show lanthanoid contraction — steady decrease in atomic/ionic radii due to poor shielding by 4f electrons, causing near-identical properties of 4d/5d elements below them.
  • Actinoids (5f, Th-Lr): show a wider range of oxidation states than lanthanoids (5f, 6d, 7s energies comparable); all are radioactive.

Exam tip

KCET usually asks 3-4 questions from this chapter: expect one on electronic configuration exceptions (Cr, Cu), one on colour/magnetic moment, one on KMnO$_4$/K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ chemistry, and one on lanthanoid contraction/oxidation states.

questions.q: The electronic configuration of Cr (Z = 24) in the ground state is
questions.explanation: Chromium adopts [Ar]3d$^5$4s$^1$ instead of 3d$^4$4s$^2$ because a half-filled d subshell (d$^5$) gives extra exchange stabilisation energy.
questions.trick: Half-filled/full-filled d gets extra stability: Cr → 3d$^5$4s$^1$, not 3d$^4$4s$^2$.

questions.q: Which ion is colourless due to a $d^0$ configuration?
questions.explanation: Sc$^{3+}$ has configuration [Ar]3d$^0$ — with no d electrons, d-d transitions are impossible, so the ion is colourless. Ti$^{3+}$(d$^1$), V$^{3+}$(d$^2$) and Cr$^{3+}$(d$^3$) are all coloured.
questions.trick: $d^0$ or $d^{10}$ configuration → no d-d transition → colourless.

questions.q: The spin-only magnetic moment of $Mn^{2+}$ (d$^5$, high spin, 5 unpaired electrons) is
questions.explanation: $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM with n = 5: $\mu = \sqrt{5\times7} = \sqrt{35} \approx 5.92$ BM.
questions.trick: $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM, n = unpaired electrons.

questions.q: Which transition metal shows the widest range of oxidation states, from +2 to +7?
questions.explanation: Manganese shows oxidation states from +2 (Mn$^{2+}$) to +7 (in KMnO$_4$), the widest range among first-row transition metals, because its 3d and 4s electrons are all of comparable energy and available for bonding.
questions.trick: Mn (group 7) spans the widest range: +2 to +7.

questions.q: In acidic medium, KMnO$_4$ oxidises Fe$^{2+}$ to Fe$^{3+}$ while being reduced to
questions.explanation: In acidic medium, $MnO_4^- + 8H^+ + 5e^- \to Mn^{2+} + 4H_2O$, a 5-electron reduction from Mn(+7) to Mn(+2).
questions.trick: Acidic KMnO$_4$: Mn$^{7+}$→Mn$^{2+}$ (5 e⁻ gained, colourless product).

questions.q: The orange colour of dichromate ion, Cr$_2$O$_7^{2-}$, changes to yellow chromate, CrO$_4^{2-}$, on
questions.explanation: Dichromate-chromate exist in a pH-dependent equilibrium: $Cr_2O_7^{2-} + 2OH^- \rightleftharpoons 2CrO_4^{2-} + H_2O$; adding alkali shifts it to the yellow chromate form.
questions.trick: Alkali pushes equilibrium orange dichromate → yellow chromate.

questions.q: Lanthanoid contraction refers to the
options: increase in oxidation states across the series
steady increase in atomic radii across the lanthanoid series
steady decrease in atomic/ionic radii across the lanthanoid series due to poor shielding by 4f electrons
sudden decrease in radii only at cerium
questions.explanation: As we move across the lanthanoids, the poorly-shielding 4f electrons cause the effective nuclear charge on outer electrons to increase steadily, leading to a gradual, cumulative contraction in radii.
questions.trick: Poor 4f shielding across lanthanoids → steady radius shrinkage.

questions.q: A major consequence of lanthanoid contraction is that
options: 4d and 5d transition elements of the same group have almost identical atomic radii and similar properties
actinoids become more reactive than lanthanoids
questions.explanation: Because of lanthanoid contraction, the atomic radii of second (4d) and third (5d) row transition elements in the same group become nearly equal (e.g. Zr and Hf), making their chemical properties very similar and hard to separate.
questions.trick: Lanthanoid contraction makes 4d and 5d congeners nearly same size (Zr≈Hf).

questions.q: Transition metals and their compounds act as good catalysts mainly because of their
options: ability to show variable oxidation states and form unstable intermediates with reactants
questions.explanation: Variable oxidation states let transition metals form intermediate complexes with reactants and provide alternative reaction pathways with lower activation energy, and their surfaces can adsorb reactant molecules (e.g. Fe in the Haber process, V$_2$O$_5$ in the Contact process).
questions.trick: Variable oxidation states + intermediate complex formation = good catalysis.

questions.q: Interstitial compounds formed by transition metals with small atoms like C, N, H are typically
options: hard, high melting, and chemically inert, retaining metallic conductivity
questions.explanation: Small non-metal atoms occupy interstitial voids in the metal lattice without disrupting the metallic bonding much, giving compounds (e.g. steel, TiC) that are hard, have high melting points and retain metallic conductivity.
questions.trick: Small atoms in interstitial voids → hard, high-melting, still metallic (steel).

questions.q: The maximum oxidation state shown by any d-block element (+8) is exhibited by
questions.explanation: Ruthenium and osmium (group 8) can attain the +8 oxidation state, e.g. in OsO$_4$, the highest oxidation state known among the d-block elements.
questions.trick: +8 is the ceiling of d-block oxidation states: only Ru and Os reach it.

questions.q: The most common and stable oxidation state of lanthanoids is
questions.explanation: Lanthanoids predominantly show the +3 oxidation state (by losing 5d$^1$6s$^2$ electrons or equivalent), which is their most stable state, though a few show +2 or +4 in special cases (e.g. Ce$^{4+}$, Eu$^{2+}$).
questions.trick: Lanthanoids default to +3 (losing 5d$^1$6s$^2$-type electrons).

questions.q: Compared to lanthanoids, actinoids show
options: a wider range of oxidation states because 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals are close in energy
a narrower range of oxidation states
questions.explanation: In actinoids the 5f, 6d and 7s energy levels are comparable, allowing more electrons to participate in bonding, so actinoids show a greater variety of oxidation states than lanthanoids.
questions.trick: Actinoids: 5f/6d/7s close in energy → wider oxidation-state range than lanthanoids.

questions.q: Zn, Cd and Hg are not regarded as typical transition elements because
options: they have completely filled $(n-1)d^{10}$ configuration in the ground state as well as common oxidation states, so they cannot show d-d transitions
questions.explanation: Zn, Cd, Hg have $d^{10}$ configuration in both the elemental and common (+2) oxidation states, so they lack partially filled d orbitals and hence do not show typical transition metal properties like colour and variable oxidation states.
questions.trick: Zn/Cd/Hg have full $d^{10}$ always → not true transition metals.

questions.q: Across the first transition series (Sc to Zn), the general trend in atomic radii is
options: a decrease initially, becoming roughly constant in the middle, then a slight increase near Cu, Zn
questions.explanation: Radii decrease initially due to increasing nuclear charge, level off around the middle (Cr-Fe) as d-electron shielding roughly balances increasing charge, and rise slightly near Cu and Zn due to increased electron-electron repulsion in the filled d subshell.
questions.trick: Radii trend across series: dip, flatten mid-series, tick up near Cu/Zn.

questions.q: K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ is manufactured industrially starting from which ore?
questions.explanation: Chromite ore (FeCr$_2$O$_4$) is fused with sodium carbonate and air to give sodium chromate, which is acidified and converted to potassium dichromate, K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$.
questions.trick: K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ traces back to chromite ore, FeCr$_2$O$_4$.

questions.q: Number of unpaired electrons in Fe$^{3+}$ (3d$^5$, high spin) and its corresponding magnetic moment are
questions.explanation: Fe$^{3+}$ is $3d^5$; in the high-spin free ion all 5 electrons are unpaired (one per orbital), giving $\mu = \sqrt{5\times7} = 5.92$ BM.
questions.trick: Fe$^{3+}$ is d$^5$ high-spin → 5 unpaired e⁻ → $\mu=5.92$ BM (same as Mn$^{2+}$).

questions.q: Which of the following statements about transition metals is INCORRECT?
options: All transition metal ions are paramagnetic
They show variable oxidation states differing usually by one unit
They generally form coloured compounds due to d-d transitions
They form a large number of complex compounds
questions.explanation: Ions with $d^0$ (e.g. Sc$^{3+}$, Ti$^{4+}$) or $d^{10}$ (e.g. Zn$^{2+}$) configurations have no unpaired electrons and are diamagnetic, so not all transition metal ions are paramagnetic.
questions.trick: $d^0$/$d^{10}$ ions (Sc$^{3+}$, Zn$^{2+}$) are diamagnetic — not all TM ions paramagnetic.

questions.q: In neutral or faintly alkaline medium, KMnO$_4$ oxidises reactants and itself is reduced to
questions.explanation: In neutral/faintly alkaline medium, $MnO_4^- + 2H_2O + 3e^- \to MnO_2 + 4OH^-$, a 3-electron reduction from Mn(+7) to Mn(+4), giving a brown MnO$_2$ precipitate.
questions.trick: Neutral/alkaline KMnO$_4$: Mn$^{7+}$→Mn$^{4+}$ (MnO$_2$, brown ppt, 3 e⁻).

questions.q: Which pair of elements is most likely to form a substitutional solid solution alloy?
options: Cu and Ni (similar atomic radii and both transition metals)
questions.explanation: Alloys form readily between transition metals of similar atomic size that can substitute for each other in the lattice, such as Cu and Ni; very small atoms like H or C instead occupy interstitial sites rather than substituting.
questions.trick: Similar-sized transition metal atoms (Cu, Ni) form substitutional alloys.

questions.q: The oxidation state of manganese in KMnO$_4$ is
questions.explanation: K is +1, each O is $-2$: $(+1)+x+4(-2)=0 \Rightarrow x=+7$.
questions.trick: Oxidation state algebra: K(+1)+Mn+4O(−2)=0 → Mn=+7.

questions.q: The oxidation state of chromium in K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ is
questions.explanation: $2(+1)+2x+7(-2)=0 \Rightarrow 2+2x-14=0 \Rightarrow x=+6$.

questions.q: Cr$^{2+}$ is a stronger reducing agent than Fe$^{2+}$ mainly because
options: oxidation of Cr$^{2+}$(d$^4$) to Cr$^{3+}$(d$^3$, half-filled $t_{2g}^3$) is thermodynamically favourable, while Fe$^{2+}$(d$^6$) to Fe$^{3+}$(d$^5$) is less so in comparison
Fe$^{2+}$ cannot be oxidised at all
questions.explanation: Cr$^{2+}$ readily loses an electron to attain the extra-stable $d^3$ ($t_{2g}^3$) configuration in Cr$^{3+}$, making Cr$^{2+}$ a good reducing agent; Fe$^{2+}$(d$^6$) is comparatively more stable and less easily oxidised.
questions.trick: Cr$^{2+}$(d$^4$)→Cr$^{3+}$(d$^3$, stable $t_{2g}^3$) drives strong reducing power.

questions.q: Mn$^{3+}$ ion in aqueous solution is unstable and tends to
options: convert entirely into MnO$_4^-$ without any other product
questions.explanation: Mn$^{3+}$(d$^4$) disproportionates in aqueous solution: $2Mn^{3+} + 2H_2O \to Mn^{2+} + MnO_2 + 4H^+$, since Mn$^{2+}$ (d$^5$, half-filled, stable) and Mn(+4) are both more stable relative to Mn$^{3+}$.
questions.trick: Mn$^{3+}$(d$^4$) disproportionates to stable Mn$^{2+}$(d$^5$) + MnO$_2$(d$^4$... Mn$^{4+}$).

questions.q: Transition metals readily form a large number of complex compounds mainly because they have
options: no ability to form coordinate bonds
large atomic size, low charge and no vacant orbitals
completely filled d-orbitals in all oxidation states
small ionic size, relatively high ionic charge, and vacant low-energy d-orbitals available to accept ligand lone pairs
questions.explanation: Their small size, high charge density and empty/partially filled d-orbitals allow transition metal ions to strongly accept electron pairs donated by ligands, favouring extensive complex (coordination compound) formation.
questions.trick: Small size + high charge + empty d-orbitals = strong ligand-accepting ability.

questions.q: Automobile catalytic converters typically use which transition metals to catalyse the oxidation of CO and unburnt hydrocarbons and the reduction of NO$_x$?
questions.explanation: Platinum, palladium and rhodium, coated on a ceramic support, act as heterogeneous catalysts in catalytic converters, promoting complete combustion of CO/hydrocarbons and reduction of nitrogen oxides.
questions.trick: Catalytic converters: remember Pt, Pd, Rh trio for CO/NOx cleanup.

questions.q: In acidic medium, the equivalent weight of KMnO$_4$ (molar mass M) used as an oxidising agent (Mn$^{7+}\to$Mn$^{2+}$) is
questions.explanation: In acidic medium MnO$_4^-$ accepts 5 electrons per formula unit (Mn$^{7+}\to$Mn$^{2+}$), so its equivalent weight is molar mass divided by 5.
questions.trick: Eq. wt of KMnO$_4$ = M/(electrons gained): acidic medium → M/5.

questions.q: In acidic medium, the equivalent weight of K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ (molar mass M) as an oxidising agent (2Cr$^{6+}\to$2Cr$^{3+}$) is
questions.explanation: One mole of Cr$_2$O$_7^{2-}$ accepts 6 electrons overall (2 Cr atoms each gaining 3 electrons), so its equivalent weight is molar mass divided by 6.
questions.trick: Eq. wt of K$_2$Cr$_2$O$_7$ = M/6 (2 Cr atoms × 3 e⁻ each).

questions.q: A KMnO$_4$ solution has a molarity of 0.02 M. Used as an oxidant in acidic medium (n-factor = 5), its normality is
questions.explanation: Normality $=$ molarity $\times$ n-factor $= 0.02\times5 = 0.10$ N.
questions.trick: Normality = Molarity × n-factor; here 0.02×5=0.10 N.

questions.q: Among the transition metals, tungsten (W) has an exceptionally high melting point mainly because
options: it has many unpaired d-electrons available for strong, extensive metallic (covalent-type) bonding
it has a completely filled d-subshell
it is the lightest transition metal
questions.explanation: Tungsten has a large number of unpaired d-electrons that participate in strong metallic bonding with significant covalent character, giving it one of the highest melting points of any metal.
questions.trick: More unpaired d-electrons → stronger metallic bonding → higher m.p. (W).

questions.q: Across the first transition series, the density of the metals generally
options: increases from Sc to Cu, since atomic mass increases while atomic volume decreases only slightly
decreases steadily due to decreasing atomic mass
shows no relationship with atomic structure
questions.explanation: As atomic number increases across the series, atomic mass rises while atomic radius decreases only slightly (levelling off in the middle), so density (mass/volume) generally increases from Sc towards the Cu/Zn end.
questions.trick: Mass rises faster than volume shrinks across the series → density increases.

questions.q: Separation of the lanthanoids from one another is difficult mainly because
options: they have widely differing oxidation states
they have almost identical ionic radii and very similar chemical properties, due to lanthanoid contraction
they do not form any soluble salts
questions.explanation: Since lanthanoids mostly show the +3 state with very similar (and gradually contracting) ionic radii, their chemical behaviour is nearly identical, making separation difficult; ion-exchange chromatography is commonly used to separate them.
questions.trick: Near-identical +3 ionic radii (lanthanoid contraction) make lanthanoids hard to separate.

questions.q: Misch metal, used in lighter flints, is an alloy consisting mainly of
options: a lanthanoid metal (mostly cerium, about 95%) along with iron and traces of S, C, Ca, Al
questions.explanation: Misch metal is approximately 95% lanthanoid metal (mainly cerium) with about 5% iron and traces of other elements; it sparks readily on friction, making it useful in cigarette lighter flints.
questions.trick: Misch metal = ~95% lanthanoid (mostly Ce) + Fe + traces — used in flints.

questions.q: Which lanthanoid commonly and stably shows a +4 oxidation state in addition to the usual +3, because the resulting ion attains a noble (f$^0$) configuration?
questions.explanation: Ce$^{4+}$ has an empty 4f subshell ($4f^0$), which is an extra-stable configuration, so cerium readily and stably shows +4 in addition to its usual +3 state (e.g. ceric ammonium sulphate, CAS, as an oxidant).
questions.trick: Ce$^{4+}$ reaches stable empty $4f^0$ → Ce is the +4-showing lanthanoid.

questions.q: Manganese has an unexpectedly high first ionisation enthalpy compared with the general trend across the first transition series, mainly because
options: Mn has the largest atomic radius in the series
Mn ($3d^54s^2$) has an extra-stable, exactly half-filled 3d subshell, requiring more energy to remove an electron
questions.explanation: The symmetric, half-filled $3d^5$ configuration of Mn has extra exchange stabilisation, so removing an electron from it (to form Mn$^+$) requires relatively more energy, giving Mn a higher first IE than expected from the smooth trend.
questions.trick: Mn's exactly half-filled $3d^5$ resists electron removal → abnormally high IE1.

questions.q: According to the IUPAC definition, a transition element is one whose atom (in the elemental state) or at least one of its simple ions has
options: a completely filled outermost d-subshell in all its compounds
questions.explanation: A transition element is defined as one having a partially filled d-subshell in the atom or in at least one of its common ions; this is why Sc (atom: $3d^14s^2$) is classed as a transition metal even though Sc$^{3+}$ is $d^0$.
questions.trick: IUPAC test: partially filled d-subshell in ATOM or ANY common ion.

questions.q: The contraction in atomic/ionic radii across the actinoid series (actinoid contraction) is GREATER, element for element, than the lanthanoid contraction mainly because
options: 5f orbitals shield more effectively than 4f orbitals
5f orbitals are more diffuse and shield the nuclear charge even more poorly than 4f orbitals do
questions.explanation: The 5f orbitals are more diffuse than 4f orbitals and shield the increasing nuclear charge even less effectively, so the actinoid contraction per element is somewhat larger than the corresponding lanthanoid contraction.
questions.trick: 5f more diffuse than 4f, shields worse → actinoid contraction > lanthanoid contraction.

questions.q: Which of the following 3d ions has exactly 3 unpaired electrons?
questions.explanation: Cr$^{3+}$ has configuration $t_{2g}^3$ ($d^3$), with one electron in each of the three $t_{2g}$ orbitals, giving 3 unpaired electrons; Mn$^{2+}$(d$^5$) has 5, and Zn$^{2+}$/Ti$^{4+}$ have none.
questions.trick: Count unpaired in $t_{2g}$/$e_g$: Cr$^{3+}$ (d$^3$) = 3 unpaired electrons.

questions.q: The spin-only magnetic moment of a metal ion with 4 unpaired electrons (e.g. high-spin Fe$^{2+}$, d$^6$) is
questions.explanation: $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM with n = 4: $\mu = \sqrt{4\times6} = \sqrt{24} \approx 4.90$ BM.
questions.trick: $\mu=\sqrt{n(n+2)}$ with n=4 → $\sqrt{24}\approx4.90$ BM.

questions.q: Which statement about the maximum oxidation states of d-block elements is CORRECT?
options: The maximum oxidation state generally corresponds to the total number of $(n-1)d$ and $ns$ electrons, rising to a peak around the middle of the series (e.g. Mn shows +7, matching its group number)
The maximum oxidation state decreases smoothly and continuously from Sc to Zn
d-block elements never show oxidation states higher than +3
The maximum oxidation state is always +2, regardless of the element
questions.explanation: Early-to-middle transition metals can use both their $(n-1)d$ and $ns$ electrons in bonding, so the maximum oxidation state tends to rise towards the group number (e.g. Mn, group 7, reaches +7 in KMnO$_4$), before falling again towards the later members like Cu and Zn.
questions.trick: Max oxidation state ≈ total (n-1)d+ns electrons, peaks near group number (Mn=+7).
